procedural_history.originating_court: Police Station Jamia Nagar, District: South-East, Delhi
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 19.01.2023 of the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi in WPCRL No. 1326 of 2022
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant approached the High Court of Delhi through a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution of India read with Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for quashing of the ‘History Sheet’ opened against him and the proposal to declare him as ‘Bad Character’ with the entry of his name in the Surveillance ‘Register-X, Part II, Bundle A’ at Police Station Jamia Nagar, District: South-East, Delhi. The Single Judge of High Court dismissed the appellant’s writ petition.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court partly allowed the appeal, modifying the High Court judgment. The Supreme Court directed that the amended Standing Order dated 21.03.2024 be given effect forthwith in the appellant’s case. The Supreme Court also directed the Commissioner of Police, Delhi to designate a senior police officer of the rank of Joint Commissioner of Police or above, to periodically audit contents of History Sheets, ensure confidentiality, and delete names of persons/children found innocent during investigation from “relations and connections” category in History Sheet and to take prompt action against any police officer acting contrary to amended Standing Order.

directions: The impugned judgment of the High Court dated 19.01.2023 stands modified.
The amended Standing Order dated 21.03.2024 be given effect forthwith in the appellant’s case.

The Commissioner of Police, Delhi is directed to designate a senior police officer of the rank of Joint Commissioner of Police or above, to periodically audit the contents of History Sheets, ensure confidentiality, and delete the names of persons/children found innocent during investigation from the “relations and connections” category in the History Sheet.
Prompt action is to be taken against any police officer acting contrary to the amended Standing Order.

issue.issue_text: Whether the names of the Appellant’s minor children and his wife against whom there is no adverse material should be included in the History Sheet of the Appellant.

facts: The appellant challenged a High Court decision that allowed his police History Sheet to include the names of his wife and minor children.
There was no adverse material or evidence of wrongdoing against the wife or the minor children.
During the proceedings, the Delhi Police issued an amended Standing Order (dated 21.03.2024) to govern the preparation of History Sheets.
law: The key legal basis for the decision was the newly amended Standing Order.

This order states that the “relations and connections” column in a History Sheet should only include names of individuals likely to provide shelter to the offender when they are wanted by the police, such as associates in crime, abettors, and receivers.

Crucially, the amended order explicitly prohibits recording the details of any minor relatives (son, daughter, siblings) unless there is specific evidence that the minor has afforded shelter to the offender while they were on the run.
The order also references Section 74 of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, which prohibits disclosing the identity of a child in conflict with the law.
application: The Court found that the amended Standing Order directly and largely addressed the appellant's grievance.

It reasoned that the new rules would prevent the "undesirable exposure" of the appellant's minor children by stopping the police from mechanically including their names simply due to their relationship with the appellant.

The Court determined that the inclusion of family members, especially minors, is only justified if there is concrete evidence that they have actively assisted the offender, such as by providing shelter.
The Court also noted that the clarification of the History Sheet as an internal, non-public document, combined with the new safeguards, was a necessary step to redress the appellant's concerns.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the appellant's argument, partly allowing the appeal. It held that the names of the appellant's minor children and wife should not be included in his History Sheet without adverse material against them. The Court directed that the newly amended Standing Order, which prohibits recording minors' names unless there is evidence they provided shelter, be applied to the appellant's case immediately to prevent their undesirable exposure.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the names of the Appellant’s minor children and his wife against whom there is no adverse material should be included in the History Sheet of the Appellant.
appellant_arguments: The inclusion of the names of the appellant's school-going minor children and his wife in his History Sheet is disturbing and constitutes undesirable exposure, especially since there is no adverse material against them.
respondent_arguments: The format of the history sheets, which includes details of family members, was prescribed and followed according to existing rules, specifically Rule 23.8 and Rule 23.9.

statutes.act_name: Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The Commissioner of Police, Delhi, must designate a senior police officer of the rank of Joint Commissioner of Police or above to periodically audit the contents of History Sheets. This audit must ensure confidentiality and the deletion of names of persons, including children, found innocent during an investigation from the 'relations and connections' category. Prompt action is to be taken against any police officer who acts contrary to the governing amended Standing Order.
obiter: All States and Union Territories should revisit their policy-regime and consider whether suitable amendments on the pattern of the 'Delhi Model' are required to be made to protect the privacy of innocent relatives of individuals with history sheets.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the amended Standing Order, which prohibits recording the details of minor relatives in a History Sheet unless there is evidence they afforded shelter to the offender, sufficiently addresses the appellant's grievance. This amendment, coupled with the policy of keeping the History Sheet as an internal police document, will prevent the undesirable exposure of the appellant's minor children.
legal_tests_applied: The expression ‘life’ under Article 21 of the Constitution includes the right to live a life worthy of human honour, which encompasses self-regard, social image, and an honest space for oneself in society.
why_respondent_won: The respondents' case was strengthened by their proactive amendment of the Standing Order during the proceedings, which addressed the court's primary concerns regarding the inclusion of minors' names.

The respondents' decision to treat the History Sheet as an internal police document that shall not be brought into the public domain was seen by the court as a measure that largely addresses the appellant's concerns about exposure.
policy_considerations: There is a need to prevent the mechanical inclusion of names of innocent individuals in History Sheets, particularly when they belong to socially, economically, and educationally disadvantaged backgrounds.

Police diaries should not be maintained selectively for individuals from certain communities (like vimukta jatis) based on caste bias, as such pre-conceived notions can impede their right to live with self-respect.
A periodic audit mechanism overseen by a senior police officer is a critical tool to review and scrutinize entries in History Sheets to check for biases and discriminatory practices.
The value for human dignity and life, deeply embedded in Article 21, requires safeguarding the self-regard and social image of individuals, which can be harmed by baseless entries in police records.
